concepts.def: A sex cell produced by meiosis that contains one set of chromosomes (n) and therefore one copy of each autosomal gene. In sexual reproduction each parent contributes one haploid gamete, so each parent passes on one allele of each gene to the offspring.

The cell formed by the fusion of two haploid gametes at fertilization. It contains two sets of chromosomes (2n), one from each parent, and so has two copies of each autosomal gene. Every body cell produced from it by mitosis carries the same two copies.

A life cycle in which haploid gametes are produced by meiosis in the parents and fuse to form a diploid zygote. This pattern of inheritance is common to all eukaryotes that reproduce sexually, including plants, fungi and animals, even though the organisms differ in which stage of the cycle is dominant.

The generations named in a genetic cross. The P (parental) generation is the pair of organisms first crossed; the F1 (first filial) generation is their offspring; the F2 (second filial) generation is produced by crossing F1 individuals with each other or by allowing them to self-fertilize.

A grid used to predict the outcome of a genetic cross. The possible gametes of one parent head the columns and those of the other parent head the rows; each cell shows a possible offspring genotype, and the cells are counted to give the expected genotypic and phenotypic ratios.

The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Pollen contains the male gametes and the female gametes are located in ovules inside the ovary, so pollination must take place before the gametes can fuse. To cross two chosen plants, the breeder transfers pollen from one plant to the stigma of the other, usually after removing the anthers of the recipient flower so that it cannot self-pollinate.

Plants such as peas produce both male and female gametes on the same plant, so pollen can be transferred to a stigma of the same plant (self-pollination) and a male gamete can then fuse with a female gamete of the same plant (self-fertilization). Self-fertilization of an F1 plant is a standard way of producing an F2 generation. Genetic crosses of this kind are widely used to breed new varieties of crop and ornamental plants.

The combination of alleles that an organism has inherited, for one gene or for many. For a single autosomal gene the genotype consists of two alleles, one inherited from each parent, and is written with two symbols such as Tt.

A gene is a length of DNA at a particular locus that codes for a polypeptide or has another specific function; an allele is one of the alternative forms of that gene, differing from other alleles in its base sequence. All the alleles of a gene occupy the same locus, so a diploid organism carries two alleles of each autosomal gene, which may be the same or different.

Having two copies of the same allele of a gene, for example TT or tt. A homozygous organism produces only one type of gamete with respect to that gene and, if self-fertilized or crossed with an identical homozygote, breeds true for the trait.

Having two different alleles of a gene, for example Tt. A heterozygous organism produces two types of gamete for that gene in equal numbers, one carrying each allele, because the two alleles segregate during meiosis.

The observable traits of an organism, including its structure, physiology and behaviour, resulting from its genotype and from environmental factors. Some human traits are due to genotype only (for example ABO blood group), some to environment only (for example scars or the language first spoken) and many to interaction between genotype and environment (for example height or skin colour).

An allele that has the same effect on the phenotype whether it is present in the homozygous or the heterozygous state. Typically a dominant allele codes for a functional protein and one copy is enough to produce the trait, so a homozygous-dominant genotype and a heterozygous genotype give the same phenotype.

An allele that affects the phenotype only when it is present in the homozygous state. Many recessive alleles code for a non-functional or absent protein; in a heterozygote the dominant allele still produces enough functional protein for the trait, so the recessive allele has no observable effect there, although it is still present and can be passed to offspring.

The capacity of an organism to develop traits suited to the environment it experiences, by varying its patterns of gene expression rather than by any change in its genotype. Because the genotype is unchanged, the altered traits may be reversible during the lifetime of the individual if the environment changes again, as with the darkening of skin on exposure to sunlight.

A human disease inherited as a recessive condition, caused by mutation in an autosomal gene that codes for the enzyme needed to convert the amino acid phenylalanine to tyrosine. A person homozygous for the mutant allele lacks a functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates and causes damage to the developing brain unless dietary phenylalanine is restricted from birth.

An individual heterozygous for a recessive disease allele who does not have the disease but can pass the allele to offspring. Two carriers of PKU are unaffected, because one functional allele produces enough enzyme, but each child they have has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting the mutant allele from both parents and having PKU.

A position in the genome at which a single nucleotide differs between individuals in a population. SNPs are the most common source of the different alleles of a gene: two alleles that differ at one SNP may code for polypeptides differing in a single amino acid, or may differ in how much the gene is expressed.

The existence of more than two alleles of a gene in a gene pool. Any number of alleles of a gene can exist in the population, because mutations at different positions produce different variants, but a diploid individual inherits only two of them, one from each parent.

All the alleles of all the genes carried by the members of an interbreeding population. The gene pool is where multiple alleles of a gene exist together, even though each individual carries at most two of them.

The gene for the ABO blood group has three alleles in the human gene pool, denoted IA, IB and i. IA and IB are codominant with each other and both are dominant to i, so the genotypes IAIA and IAi give group A, IBIB and IBi give group B, IAIB gives group AB and ii gives group O.

A pattern of inheritance in which both alleles of a heterozygote are fully expressed, so the heterozygote has a dual phenotype showing the effects of both alleles at once. The AB blood type (genotype IAIB) is an example: both the A and the B antigens are present on the red blood cells.

A pattern of inheritance in which the heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes, because neither allele is fully dominant. In the four o'clock flower or marvel of Peru (Mirabilis jalapa), red-flowered and white-flowered homozygotes produce pink-flowered heterozygotes, and pink × pink gives red, pink and white offspring in a 1:2:1 ratio.

Humans have one pair of sex chromosomes: XX in females and XY in males. Every egg carries an X chromosome, whereas a sperm carries either an X or a Y, so it is the sex chromosome in the sperm that determines whether the zygote develops male-typical or female-typical physical characteristics. The X chromosome carries far more genes than the much smaller Y chromosome.

A gene located on a sex chromosome, in practice almost always the X chromosome because it carries far more genes than the Y. Males have only one X chromosome, so they have a single copy of each X-linked gene and a single recessive allele produces the recessive phenotype; females have two copies. Alleles on the X chromosome are shown as superscript letters on an uppercase X, for example XH and Xh, and a male genotype is written XHY or XhY.

A sex-linked genetic disorder in which blood fails to clot normally, caused by a recessive allele (Xh) of a gene on the X chromosome. A male with genotype XhY has haemophilia because he has no second X chromosome to carry the dominant allele; a female XHXh is an unaffected carrier, and an affected female (XhXh) is rare because she must inherit Xh from both parents. Sons receive their X chromosome from their mother, so a carrier mother passes the allele to half her sons on average.

A diagram showing the family relationships and phenotypes of individuals over several generations, used to deduce the pattern of inheritance of a genetic disorder. For example, an affected child born to two unaffected parents shows that the condition is recessive and that both parents are heterozygous; an affected daughter with an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive inheritance. Because close relatives are more likely to carry the same recessive allele inherited from a common ancestor, marriage between close relatives raises the chance of children being homozygous for a recessive disorder, which is the genetic basis for its prohibition in many societies.

Reasoning that draws a general conclusion from observations of some but not all cases. Scientists use it when they base a theory on the cases they have observed, for example deducing that a disorder is inherited as an autosomal recessive condition from the pattern seen in part of a pedigree chart.

Reasoning from a general principle or theory to a conclusion about a specific case. Once a pattern of inheritance has been proposed for a pedigree, it can be used deductively to work out the genotypes of specific individuals, for example that the unaffected parents of an affected child must both be heterozygous.

Variation in a trait that can take any value within a range, with no distinct categories, so that a population shows a continuous distribution of values. It results from polygenic inheritance, from environmental factors, or from both: human skin colour is continuously variable because several genes each contribute to the amount of melanin and exposure to sunlight also affects it.

The control of a single trait by two or more genes, each usually with a small additive effect. Because many combinations of alleles are possible, polygenic traits such as human skin colour show many phenotypes grading into one another rather than a few discrete classes.

A variable that falls into a limited number of separate categories with no intermediates, such as ABO blood group (A, B, AB or O). Discrete variables are usually controlled by one gene, whereas continuous variables such as skin colour or height take any value across a range.

Measures of central tendency for a set of values. The mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value when the values are arranged in order (or the mean of the two middle values); the mode is the value that occurs most often. For a continuous variable the mean is the usual measure, but the median is less affected by outliers.

A plot that displays six aspects of data for a continuous variable such as student height: the minimum, the first quartile, the median, the third quartile, the maximum and any outliers. The box extends from the first quartile to the third quartile with a line at the median; the whiskers extend to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers, and outliers are plotted as separate points.

The interquartile range (IQR) is the difference between the third quartile and the first quartile and contains the middle half of the data. A data point is categorized as an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile or more than 1.5 × IQR below the first quartile.

The separation of the two alleles of a gene into different gametes during meiosis, because the homologous chromosomes carrying them are pulled to opposite poles in anaphase I. A heterozygote Aa therefore produces gametes carrying A and gametes carrying a in equal numbers.

The random orientation of each bivalent on the equator in metaphase I of meiosis, independently of every other bivalent, so that the alleles of genes on different chromosomes are combined at random in the gametes. A double heterozygote AaBb for two unlinked genes therefore produces the gametes AB, Ab, aB and ab in equal proportions, which is the basis of the ratios seen in dihybrid crosses.

A cross that follows the inheritance of two genes at once. For two unlinked autosomal genes, a cross between two double heterozygotes (AaBb × AaBb) gives a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio, derived by combining the 3:1 ratio for each gene (3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16, 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16, 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16, 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16). A test cross of a double heterozygote with a double homozygous recessive (AaBb × aabb) gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio, because the four equally frequent gametes of the heterozygote each combine with the single gamete type ab.

The law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes assort independently of one another during gamete formation. The 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1 dihybrid ratios rest on this law, which holds only if the genes are on different chromosomes or are far enough apart on one chromosome for the recombination rate to reach 50%. Linked genes are an exception, illustrating that biological laws hold only under certain conditions.

The specific position of a gene on a particular chromosome. The locus of a human gene is the same in every individual, and a genome database records each gene's chromosome, its position on that chromosome and the polypeptide it codes for. Two genes may have loci on different chromosomes, in which case they are unlinked, or loci in close proximity on the same chromosome, in which case they are linked.

The tendency of alleles of two genes to be inherited together because their loci are on the same autosome. Alleles of linked genes do not assort independently: the combination on each chromosome is passed on intact unless crossing over between the two loci in prophase I separates them, and the closer the loci the less often this happens. In crosses the allele symbols are shown alongside vertical lines representing the homologous chromosomes.

A gamete, or an offspring genotype or phenotype, that has a combination of alleles of two genes different from the combinations in the parents. For unlinked genes recombinants arise by independent assortment and make up half the offspring of a test cross; for linked genes they arise only by crossing over between the loci and are the two less frequent classes of offspring.

A cross between an individual heterozygous for both genes and an individual homozygous recessive for both genes. Because the homozygous recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles, the phenotype of each offspring reveals which gamete it received from the heterozygous parent, so the proportions of parental and recombinant phenotypes among the offspring equal the proportions of parental and recombinant gametes.

A statistical test of whether observed results differ significantly from those expected under a hypothesis. For each class, (observed − expected)² / expected is calculated and the values are summed to give chi-squared; the degrees of freedom are the number of classes minus one. If the calculated value exceeds the critical value at p = 0.05 the null hypothesis is rejected; if it is smaller, the null hypothesis is not rejected and the observed results are consistent with the expected ratio.

In a chi-squared test on a dihybrid cross, the null hypothesis (H0) states that there is no significant difference between the observed and expected numbers, so any difference is due to chance and the genes assort independently. The alternative hypothesis (H1) states that the observed results differ significantly from the expected ratio, for example because the genes are linked.

A difference is statistically significant at the p = 0.05 level if the probability of obtaining a difference at least as large by chance alone, when the null hypothesis is true, is less than 5%. Statistical testing uses a sample to represent a population: in a dihybrid cross the sample is the F2 generation counted, and in many experiments it is the set of replicated or repeated measurements.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the means of inheritance in eukaryotes that have a sexual life cycle?
options: Each parent produces haploid gametes by meiosis, and their fusion forms a diploid zygote with two copies of each autosomal gene
Each parent's gametes carry both of its alleles of every gene, so the zygote's traits blend the two parental genotypes
Haploid gametes fusing to form a zygote is the pattern in animals, while plants pass on their genes through pollen and seeds instead
Each gamete carries the parent's single copy of each gene, so the zygote formed at fertilization has one copy of each gene
mcqs.specStatementText: Haploid gametes fuse to make a diploid zygote
mcqs.explain: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that each gamete carries one copy of each autosomal gene; fertilization restores the diploid number, giving the zygote two copies, one from each parent. This pattern is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.
rationales: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that each gamete carries one copy of each autosomal gene; fertilization restores the diploid number, giving the zygote two copies, one from each parent. This pattern is common to all sexually reproducing eukaryotes.

A student who thinks a parent passes on its whole genotype picks this. Gametes are haploid and carry only one allele of each gene, chosen at random in meiosis, and the alleles remain separate in the zygote rather than blending.

A student who files plant reproduction as a separate process picks this. Pollen contains male gametes and the ovule contains the female gamete; their fusion forms a diploid zygote, so plants follow the same haploid–diploid pattern as animals.

A student who pictures a gene as a single object in the cell picks this. A diploid parent has two copies of each autosomal gene and puts one into each gamete; the zygote therefore has two copies, one on each homologous chromosome.

mcqs.q: A breeder wants to cross a tall pea plant with a dwarf pea plant to obtain an F1 generation. Which procedure is required, and why?
options: Place pollen from one plant on the stigma of the other, where it fuses with the female gamete, so there is no need to remove the anthers first
Remove the anthers from flowers of one plant, then transfer pollen from the other plant to their stigmas, because a pea flower would otherwise self-pollinate
Grow the two plants next to each other, because a pea flower cannot be fertilized by its own pollen and so has to be cross-pollinated by insects
Allow the tall plant to self-pollinate and cross its seedlings with the dwarf plant, because the F1 is produced from a parent's own offspring
mcqs.specStatementText: How a plant cross is done
mcqs.explain: Peas produce male and female gametes on the same plant and normally self-pollinate. To make a cross the breeder must prevent selfing by removing the anthers and then carry out pollination by hand, transferring pollen (which contains the male gametes) to the stigma so that a pollen tube can reach the female gametes in the ovary.
rationales: A student who thinks the pollen grain is the gamete and that fertilization happens on the stigma picks this. The female gametes are in the ovary, and unless the anthers are removed the flower's own pollen may fertilize them, spoiling the cross.

Peas produce male and female gametes on the same plant and normally self-pollinate. To make a cross the breeder must prevent selfing by removing the anthers and then carry out pollination by hand, transferring pollen (which contains the male gametes) to the stigma so that a pollen tube can reach the female gametes in the ovary.

A student who assumes an organism cannot fertilize itself picks this. Peas readily self-pollinate and self-fertilize, which is exactly why the breeder has to intervene to obtain a cross between two different plants.

A student who has confused the generation labels picks this. The F1 generation is the direct offspring of the P generation cross between the tall and dwarf plants; no intermediate selfing is involved.

mcqs.q: A pea plant has the genotype Tt for the gene controlling stem height. Which statement about this plant is correct?
options: It has two separate genes controlling stem height, called T and t
It is heterozygous because its phenotype differs from both its parents
It is heterozygous, since it has two different alleles of one gene
It carries only the T allele in its body cells, with t only in its gametes
mcqs.explain: T and t are two alleles, alternative forms of the one gene for stem height, occupying the same locus on the two homologous chromosomes. Having two different alleles is the definition of heterozygous.
rationales: A student who uses gene and allele as synonyms picks this. There is one gene for stem height; T and t are alleles, different versions of that gene, and the genotype is the combination of alleles inherited.

A student who attaches 'hetero' to the parents rather than to the alleles picks this. Heterozygous describes the two alleles of a gene being different, whatever the parents looked like; a Tt plant is tall, like a TT plant.
T and t are two alleles, alternative forms of the one gene for stem height, occupying the same locus on the two homologous chromosomes. Having two different alleles is the definition of heterozygous.
A student who thinks a cell holds a single copy of each gene picks this. Every diploid body cell of the plant carries both T and t; meiosis then places one or the other into each haploid gamete.

mcqs.q: Which list gives a human trait due to genotype only, then a trait due to environment only, then a trait due to interaction between genotype and environment, in that order?
options: Adult height; a facial scar; skin colour
ABO blood group; adult height; a facial scar
ABO blood group; skin colour; adult height
ABO blood group; a scar; adult height
mcqs.explain: ABO blood group is set entirely by the alleles inherited; a scar has no genetic basis; adult height depends on the alleles inherited and on environmental factors such as nutrition during growth, so it results from interaction between genotype and environment.
rationales: A student who thinks inherited traits are fixed by the genes alone files height as genotype only. Height is strongly influenced by nutrition and health during growth, so it is an interaction trait, not a genotype-only one.

A student who treats any observable trait as part of the heritable phenotype puts the scar with the traits that involve genotype. A scar is due to the environment only, and height, listed here as environment only, has a clear genetic component.

A student who credits sunlight with all variation in skin colour puts it as environment only. Skin colour depends on several genes as well as on exposure to sunlight, so it is an interaction trait, like height.

ABO blood group is set entirely by the alleles inherited; a scar has no genetic basis; adult height depends on the alleles inherited and on environmental factors such as nutrition during growth, so it results from interaction between genotype and environment.

mcqs.q: In peas the allele T for tall stems is dominant to the allele t for dwarf stems, and TT and Tt plants are equally tall. What is the reason that the heterozygote is not shorter than the homozygous dominant plant?
options: One T allele makes enough functional protein for full stem growth, so the t allele has no observable effect
The T allele switches off the t allele in the heterozygote, so the plant effectively has two working T alleles
Tall plants are more common than dwarf plants, so the tall allele is the stronger one and takes over
The heterozygote is in fact slightly shorter, because a single T allele makes half as much of the protein as two
mcqs.specStatementText: Why one dominant allele is enough
mcqs.explain: This is why a homozygous-dominant genotype and a heterozygous genotype produce the same phenotype: the dominant allele codes for a functional protein and a single copy makes enough of it, while the recessive allele contributes a non-functional or absent product.
rationales: This is why a homozygous-dominant genotype and a heterozygous genotype produce the same phenotype: the dominant allele codes for a functional protein and a single copy makes enough of it, while the recessive allele contributes a non-functional or absent product.

A student who imagines dominance as one allele suppressing the other picks this. The t allele is not switched off or altered; it simply makes a product that does not contribute, and one T allele is sufficient on its own.
A student who equates dominance with frequency or strength picks this. Dominance is defined by the phenotype of the heterozygote, and has nothing to do with how common an allele is in the population.

A student who reasons that one allele must give half the effect picks this, but the stem says the plants are equally tall. With complete dominance one allele produces enough protein for the full phenotype; a reduced amount does not reduce the trait.

mcqs.q: A person's skin darkens after several weeks in strong sunlight and returns to its previous colour over the winter. How is this change best explained?
options: It is phenotypic plasticity: ultraviolet light causes mutations in the melanin genes, which produce extra pigment until the mutations are repaired in winter
Phenotypic plasticity: sunlight alters the expression of genes for melanin production, and the change reverses because the genotype is unchanged
It is an adaptation acquired during life, and because it is adaptive it will be permanent and passed on to the person's children
It is a trait due to environment only, so it forms no part of the person's phenotype and involves no change in gene expression
mcqs.specStatementText: Phenotypic plasticity: adjusting without changing genes
mcqs.explain: Phenotypic plasticity is the capacity to develop traits suited to the environment experienced by varying patterns of gene expression. The alleles are exactly as inherited, so when the environmental signal is removed the expression pattern, and the trait, can revert.
rationales: A student who thinks a new trait needs a change in the genes picks this. Phenotypic plasticity is not due to changes in genotype; the base sequences of the alleles are unaltered and only their expression changes.

Phenotypic plasticity is the capacity to develop traits suited to the environment experienced by varying patterns of gene expression. The alleles are exactly as inherited, so when the environmental signal is removed the expression pattern, and the trait, can revert.

A student who applies the evolutionary sense of adaptation to an individual picks this. The stem itself shows the change reverses, and since the genotype is unchanged the tan cannot be inherited by offspring.

A student who thinks only inherited traits count as phenotype picks this. Phenotype includes all observable traits however they arise, and a tan is produced by increased expression of the genes for melanin synthesis in response to light.

mcqs.q: PKU usually appears in a child whose parents are both unaffected. Which statement correctly describes phenylketonuria (PKU)?
options: It is caused by a dominant allele of an autosomal gene, which is why the condition is expressed in every person who carries it
It is caused by a recessive allele that prevents the body making phenylalanine, so affected people need extra phenylalanine in their diet
It is caused by a recessive allele of an autosomal gene coding for the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine
It is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome, so it is expressed in males far more often than in females
mcqs.explain: PKU is a recessive genetic condition due to mutation in an autosomal gene for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. A homozygous recessive person lacks the functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates.
rationales: A student who reasons that a condition that is expressed must be dominant picks this. PKU appears only in people homozygous for the mutant allele; heterozygous carriers are unaffected, which is the signature of a recessive allele.

A student who takes the name to mean a shortage of phenylalanine picks this. The missing enzyme converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates and the treatment is a diet low in phenylalanine, not rich in it.

PKU is a recessive genetic condition due to mutation in an autosomal gene for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. A homozygous recessive person lacks the functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates.

A student who assumes that any recessive disorder appearing in the children of unaffected parents is sex-linked picks this. The PKU gene is autosomal, so the condition is equally frequent in males and females.

mcqs.q: A man and a woman are both unaffected carriers of the PKU allele. They already have one child with PKU. What is the probability that their next child will have PKU?
mcqs.explain: Both parents are heterozygous (Pp × Pp). The Punnett grid gives PP, Pp, pP and pp, so each fertilization has a 1 in 4 chance of producing a homozygous recessive child with PKU. Each child is an independent event, so the earlier affected child makes no difference.
rationales: A student who treats the 2 in 4 heterozygous carriers as the children who 'have' PKU picks this. Carriers are unaffected, because one functional allele produces enough enzyme; only the 1 in 4 homozygous recessive (pp) children have PKU.

A student who believes PKU is caused by a dominant allele expects three quarters of the children of two heterozygotes to be affected. PKU is recessive, so only the homozygous recessive quarter is affected.

A student who reads a 3:1 ratio as a quota picks this, thinking the family has already had its one affected child in four. Each fertilization is independent; the probability is 1 in 4 for every child regardless of earlier children.

Both parents are heterozygous (Pp × Pp). The Punnett grid gives PP, Pp, pP and pp, so each fertilization has a 1 in 4 chance of producing a homozygous recessive child with PKU. Each child is an independent event, so the earlier affected child makes no difference.

mcqs.q: A gene in a human population has eleven known alleles, which differ from one another at single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Which statement is correct?
options: All eleven alleles can exist in the gene pool, but any one individual inherits at most two of them
Only two of the eleven can be true alleles, one dominant and one recessive; the rest must be alleles of other genes
An individual can carry several of the eleven alleles at once, since each SNP creates a separate copy of the gene
The eleven alleles are found at eleven different loci, since each allele has a different base sequence
mcqs.specStatementText: Many alleles in the gene pool, two in each person
mcqs.explain: Any number of alleles of a gene can exist in a gene pool because mutations, including SNPs, have arisen in different lineages. A diploid individual has two copies of the locus, one from each parent, and so carries at most two different alleles.
rationales: Any number of alleles of a gene can exist in a gene pool because mutations, including SNPs, have arisen in different lineages. A diploid individual has two copies of the locus, one from each parent, and so carries at most two different alleles.
A student who has generalised from introductory two-allele crosses picks this. Multiple alleles of one gene are common; the ABO gene has three and many human genes have far more.

A student who confuses multiple alleles in a population with multiple alleles in a person picks this. A SNP is a variation at one nucleotide position within the same locus; it does not add copies, and an individual still has just two.
A student who thinks different forms of a gene must sit in different places picks this. All alleles of a gene occupy the same locus; they differ in base sequence, not in position.

mcqs.q: A woman with blood group A whose genotype is IAi has children with a man of blood group B whose genotype is IBi. Which blood groups are possible in their children, and with what probabilities?
options: Groups A, B and AB, each 1 in 3, but not group O, as neither parent is group O
Groups AB, A, B and O are all possible, each with a probability of 1 in 4
Groups A and AB only, each 1 in 2, because the IA allele is dominant to IB
Groups A and B only, each 1 in 2, since each parent passes on its own group's allele
mcqs.explain: The Punnett grid for IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), one cell each. IA and IB are codominant and both dominant to i, so all four ABO groups are possible with equal probability.
rationales: A student who thinks a child's blood group must match a parent's picks this. Both parents carry the recessive allele i, and an ii child, group O, is produced in 1 in 4 fertilizations.

The Punnett grid for IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), one cell each. IA and IB are codominant and both dominant to i, so all four ABO groups are possible with equal probability.
A student who forces the three alleles into a dominant/recessive hierarchy picks this. IA and IB are codominant, so IAIB is group AB, and IBi is group B; the option also ignores the ii children.

A student who treats blood group as a unit trait that a child takes from one parent or the other picks this. Each parent is heterozygous and passes on either of its two alleles with equal probability, so four genotypes, IAIB, IAi, IBi and ii, are possible, giving all four blood groups.

mcqs.q: In the four o'clock plant Mirabilis jalapa, a cross between a red-flowered plant and a white-flowered plant gives only pink-flowered offspring. Two of these pink plants are crossed. What phenotypes are expected in their offspring?
options: Pink only, because the red and white alleles have merged into a pink allele
Pink and white in a 3:1 ratio, because pink is dominant to white
Red, pink and white flowers in a 1:2:1 ratio, as both alleles persist
Flowers with red and white patches, because both alleles are expressed
mcqs.explain: Flower colour shows incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate. Each pink plant (CRCW) produces CR and CW gametes in equal numbers, so the cross gives CRCR red, CRCW pink and CWCW white in a 1:2:1 ratio, recovering both parental phenotypes.
rationales: A student who thinks the intermediate phenotype means the alleles have blended picks this. Alleles are discrete: the pink plants still carry one red and one white allele, and red and white reappear in the next generation.

A student who judges the phenotype seen in the heterozygote to be the dominant one picks this. Neither allele is dominant; pink exists only in heterozygotes, so a pink × pink cross also gives red homozygotes.

Flower colour shows incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is intermediate. Each pink plant (CRCW) produces CR and CW gametes in equal numbers, so the cross gives CRCR red, CRCW pink and CWCW white in a 1:2:1 ratio, recovering both parental phenotypes.

A student who has merged codominance with incomplete dominance picks this. A dual phenotype with both traits shown separately is codominance; in Mirabilis jalapa the heterozygote is uniformly pink, an intermediate phenotype.

mcqs.q: In the ABO system the red blood cells of a person with genotype IAIB carry both the A antigen and the B antigen. In Mirabilis jalapa a heterozygote for the flower-colour alleles has pink petals. What do these observations show about the two patterns of inheritance?
options: Both are examples of the same pattern, in which the alleles are mixed in the heterozygote, so AB and pink are both intermediate phenotypes
Blood group AB shows that IA is dominant to IB, while pink petals show that the red allele is dominant to the white allele
Pink is codominance, since both alleles contribute to the colour; AB is incomplete dominance, because the phenotype is between A and B
Blood group AB is codominance, since both alleles are fully expressed together; pink is incomplete dominance, since the heterozygote is intermediate
mcqs.explain: The two patterns differ at the phenotypic level. In codominance the heterozygote has a dual phenotype, both antigens present; in incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, neither red nor white. The AB blood type and Mirabilis jalapa are the guide's examples of each.
rationales: A student who files both as 'blending' picks this. Group AB is not intermediate between A and B: both antigens are present in full, which is a dual phenotype. Pink petals are intermediate, with neither allele fully expressed.

A student who expects every pair of alleles to show simple dominance picks this. If IA were dominant to IB the cells would carry only the A antigen, and if red were dominant the heterozygote would be red, not pink.

A student who has the two terms reversed picks this. Codominance means both phenotypes appear separately and completely, as with the A and B antigens; a uniformly pink flower is a single intermediate phenotype, which is incomplete dominance.

The two patterns differ at the phenotypic level. In codominance the heterozygote has a dual phenotype, both antigens present; in incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, neither red nor white. The AB blood type and Mirabilis jalapa are the guide's examples of each.

mcqs.q: Which statement about sex determination and the sex chromosomes in humans is correct?
options: The sex chromosome carried by the sperm determines the sex of the zygote, and the X chromosome carries far more genes than the Y
The sex chromosome carried by the egg determines the sex of the zygote, and the X chromosome carries far more genes than the Y does
The sex chromosome carried by the sperm determines the sex of the zygote, and the X and Y chromosomes carry the same genes
Both parents contribute equally to determining the sex of the zygote, and the Y chromosome carries far more genes than the X
mcqs.explain: All eggs carry an X chromosome, whereas a sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm decides whether the zygote is XX or XY. The Y chromosome is much smaller and carries far fewer genes than the X.
rationales: All eggs carry an X chromosome, whereas a sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm decides whether the zygote is XX or XY. The Y chromosome is much smaller and carries far fewer genes than the X.

A student who assumes the mother decides the child's characteristics picks this. Every egg carries an X, so the egg cannot vary the outcome; it is the X or Y in the sperm that determines the sex of the zygote.

A student who treats X and Y as a fully homologous pair picks this. The Y is much smaller than the X and carries relatively few genes; most X-linked genes have no counterpart on the Y, so males have a single copy of them.
A student who reasons that both parents contribute a sex chromosome and so both decide picks this. Only the sperm varies between X and Y, and it is the X, not the Y, that carries far more genes.

mcqs.q: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XHXh) has children with a man who does not have haemophilia (XHY). Their first child is a boy. What is the probability that he has haemophilia?
mcqs.explain: A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X from his mother. The mother passes XH or Xh with equal probability, so half of sons on average are XhY and have haemophilia.
rationales: A student who takes the 1 in 4 from the whole Punnett grid (XHXH, XHXh, XHY, XhY) and applies it to a son picks this. Among sons only, the two possibilities are XHY and XhY, so the probability is 1 in 2.
A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X from his mother. The mother passes XH or Xh with equal probability, so half of sons on average are XhY and have haemophilia.

A student who believes a carrier mother passes the condition to all of her sons picks this. She has one XH and one Xh and passes either with equal probability, so only half of her sons are expected to be affected.

A student who thinks haemophilia passes from father to son, and notes that this father is unaffected, picks this. A son inherits his X chromosome from his mother, so a carrier mother can have affected sons whatever the father's genotype.

mcqs.q: Why is haemophilia far more common in males than in females?
options: The allele is carried on the Y chromosome, so that a father passes the condition directly to each one of his sons
Females who inherit the allele can only ever be carriers, because the female body cannot develop the condition
Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele produces the condition, whereas a female needs two
The Y chromosome carries a second copy of the gene that is more often mutated than the copy on the X
mcqs.explain: The haemophilia allele is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male XhY has no second X to carry a dominant allele, so he has haemophilia; a female must be XhXh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother and is therefore rare.
rationales: A student who expects a male-biased condition to pass from father to son picks this. The gene is on the X chromosome; a father gives his Y to sons, so sons inherit the haemophilia allele only from their mother.

A student who believes females cannot have haemophilia picks this. A female with two Xh alleles does have haemophilia; the condition is rare in females because inheriting Xh from both parents is much less likely.

The haemophilia allele is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male XhY has no second X to carry a dominant allele, so he has haemophilia; a female must be XhXh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother and is therefore rare.

A student who thinks the X and Y carry the same genes picks this. The Y chromosome carries far fewer genes than the X and has no copy of the haemophilia gene, which is precisely why males have only one copy.

mcqs.q: A man and a woman who are both unaffected by a genetic disorder have three children: an affected daughter, an unaffected son and an unaffected daughter. The affected daughter later has four children with an unaffected man, and all four are unaffected. What can be deduced about the disorder?
options: It is autosomal dominant, because the daughter shows the disorder while her parents are merely carriers
It is X-linked recessive, since the disorder skipped a generation and none of the affected daughter's children show it
It arose as a new mutation in the daughter, because parents who do not show a disorder cannot pass it on
It is autosomal recessive, and both parents of the affected daughter must be heterozygous carriers
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading a pedigree, and inductive versus deductive reasoning
mcqs.explain: Unaffected parents with an affected child shows the allele is recessive and that both parents carry it. An affected daughter must have received a recessive allele from her father; had the gene been X-linked her father would have been affected, so the gene is autosomal. Her unaffected children are expected if her partner is homozygous dominant.
rationales: A student who links 'appears in the child' with 'dominant' picks this. A dominant allele is expressed in everyone who carries it, so an affected child would have an affected parent; carriers who show nothing are heterozygous for a recessive allele.

A student who treats any skipped generation as a sign of sex linkage picks this. An X-linked recessive disorder in a daughter requires her father to carry, and therefore show, the allele; her father is unaffected, so the gene must be autosomal.

A student who thinks the recessive allele is eliminated in an unaffected heterozygote picks this. The allele is intact in each carrier parent and is placed in half their gametes; the daughter received it from both, so no new mutation is needed.

Unaffected parents with an affected child shows the allele is recessive and that both parents carry it. An affected daughter must have received a recessive allele from her father; had the gene been X-linked her father would have been affected, so the gene is autosomal. Her unaffected children are expected if her partner is homozygous dominant.

mcqs.q: Many societies prohibit marriage between close relatives. What is the genetic basis for this prohibition?
options: Reproduction between close relatives causes new mutations, producing genetic disorders that were not present in the family beforehand
Close relatives are more likely to carry the same recessive allele inherited from a common ancestor, so their children are more likely to be homozygous for it
Recessive alleles that were switched off in each parent become active again when the same allele arrives from both sides of the family
Children of close relatives may inherit more than two alleles of a gene, which disrupts the normal dominant and recessive pattern
mcqs.specStatementText: Reading a pedigree, and inductive versus deductive reasoning
mcqs.explain: Everyone carries some harmful recessive alleles that have no effect in a heterozygote. Two relatives may both have inherited the same one from a shared ancestor, so the chance that a child receives it from both parents, and so has the disorder, is raised.
rationales: A student who reaches for mutation as the cause of any genetic harm picks this. No new mutation is involved; the risk comes from existing recessive alleles being inherited from both sides of the family.

Everyone carries some harmful recessive alleles that have no effect in a heterozygote. Two relatives may both have inherited the same one from a shared ancestor, so the chance that a child receives it from both parents, and so has the disorder, is raised.

A student who imagines the dominant allele switching off the recessive one picks this. The recessive allele is never inactivated; it simply has no observable effect in a heterozygote, and it is expressed when a child is homozygous for it.

A student who confuses multiple alleles in a population with multiple alleles in a person picks this. Any child inherits exactly two alleles of each autosomal gene, one from each parent, whether or not the parents are related.

mcqs.q: Human skin colour varies continuously across a population, whereas ABO blood group falls into four separate classes. Which explanation of this difference is correct?
options: Skin colour is controlled by one gene with a very large number of alleles, whereas the blood group gene has only three alleles
Skin colour is determined by the environment only, with no genetic contribution, whereas blood group is determined by genotype only
Skin colour depends on several genes and on sunlight, giving many grades; blood group depends on one gene with discrete alleles
Both are continuous variables, but blood group is recorded in four categories only because the test used cannot detect intermediate values
mcqs.explain: Continuous variation is due to polygenic inheritance and/or environmental factors. Several genes each add to the amount of melanin and exposure to sunlight alters it further, so skin colour is a continuous variable; ABO blood group depends on the two alleles of one gene and is a discrete variable with four categories.
rationales: A student who confuses multiple alleles with polygenic inheritance picks this. However many alleles a gene has, an individual carries only two, so one gene gives a small number of phenotypes; continuous variation needs many genes acting together.

A student who credits sunlight with all the variation picks this. Skin colour has a strong genetic component from several genes; the environment adds to it, which is why it is an example of interaction between genotype and environment.

Continuous variation is due to polygenic inheritance and/or environmental factors. Several genes each add to the amount of melanin and exposure to sunlight alters it further, so skin colour is a continuous variable; ABO blood group depends on the two alleles of one gene and is a discrete variable with four categories.

A student who judges by how data are recorded rather than by whether intermediates exist picks this. There are no intermediate blood groups: a person's red cells carry the A antigen, the B antigen, both or neither, so blood group is a discrete variable.

mcqs.q: The heights in centimetres of nine students are: 150, 152, 152, 155, 158, 160, 163, 170 and 175. What are the mean, median and mode of these heights?
options: Mean 158 cm, median 159.4 cm, and mode 152 cm
Mean of 159.4 cm, median 152 cm, mode 158 cm
Mean 158.6 cm, with median 158 cm and mode 152 cm
Mean 159.4 cm, median 158 cm, mode 152 cm
mcqs.explain: The nine values sum to 1435, and 1435 / 9 = 159.4 (to one decimal place). The values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158. The only value that appears twice is 152, so it is the mode.
rationales: A student who thinks the median is the calculated average and the mean is the middle value swaps the two. The mean is the sum divided by the number of values, 159.4; the median is the middle value in order, 158.

A student who takes the mode to be the middle value and the median to be the most frequent value swaps those two. The median is the middle value, 158; the mode is the value that occurs most often, 152.

A student who treats the highest and lowest values as outliers and discards both before calculating picks this: (1435 − 175 − 150) / 7 = 158.6. A value is an outlier only if it lies more than 1.5 × IQR beyond a quartile; by that rule none of these nine values is an outlier, and the mean of the full data set is 159.4 cm.

The nine values sum to 1435, and 1435 / 9 = 159.4 (to one decimal place). The values are already in order, so the median is the fifth value, 158. The only value that appears twice is 152, so it is the mode.

mcqs.q: For a class's heights, the first quartile is 150 cm, the median is 158 cm, the third quartile is 166 cm, and the minimum and maximum are 130 cm and 192 cm. Above what height would a data point be categorized as an outlier on a box-and-whisker plot?
options: 190 cm
182 cm
174 cm
259 cm
mcqs.explain: The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1 = 166 − 150 = 16 cm, so 1.5 × IQR = 24 cm. A point is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile: 166 + 24 = 190 cm. The maximum of 192 cm is therefore an outlier and would be plotted separately.
rationales: The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1 = 166 − 150 = 16 cm, so 1.5 × IQR = 24 cm. A point is an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile: 166 + 24 = 190 cm. The maximum of 192 cm is therefore an outlier and would be plotted separately.
A student who measures 1.5 × IQR from the median rather than from the third quartile gets 158 + 24 = 182 cm. The rule uses the quartiles: the upper limit is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
A student who adds 1.5 × IQR to the first quartile instead of the third gets 150 + 24 = 174 cm. The upper limit is measured from the third quartile, and the lower limit from the first.

A student who takes the range (192 − 130 = 62 cm) as the interquartile range gets 1.5 × 62 = 93 and 166 + 93 = 259 cm. The IQR is the length of the box, Q3 − Q1 = 16 cm, not the full range of the data.

mcqs.q: A plant is heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes (AaBb). Which event in meiosis determines which allele of the first gene ends up in a gamete together with which allele of the second gene?
options: Crossing over between the two genes during prophase I, which exchanges alleles between chromosomes to make the four combinations
The random orientation of each bivalent on the equator at metaphase I, which is independent of the orientation of the other bivalent
The separation of sister chromatids at anaphase II, which sends the two alleles of each gene into two different gametes
The parental origin of the chromosomes, so that alleles from the plant's mother are packaged together and those from its father together
mcqs.specStatementText: Segregation and independent assortment come from meiosis
mcqs.explain: Which homologue of the A pair faces a given pole has no influence on which homologue of the B pair faces it. The alleles then segregate at anaphase I, so the four combinations AB, Ab, aB and ab are produced in equal proportions: this is independent assortment, the basis of dihybrid ratios.
rationales: A student who credits crossing over with all reshuffling picks this. Crossing over exchanges segments between homologues of the same pair; it cannot move an allele of gene A onto the chromosome carrying gene B, which is a different chromosome.

Which homologue of the A pair faces a given pole has no influence on which homologue of the B pair faces it. The alleles then segregate at anaphase I, so the four combinations AB, Ab, aB and ab are produced in equal proportions: this is independent assortment, the basis of dihybrid ratios.

A student who places the shuffling at the most memorable separation event picks this. Sister chromatids carry identical alleles (apart from crossing over); the alleles of a heterozygote are separated when homologues part at anaphase I, and the combinations are fixed by orientation at metaphase I.

A student who thinks maternal and paternal chromosomes move as sets picks this. Each bivalent orients independently, so a gamete receives a random mixture of maternal and paternal chromosomes and all four allele combinations are equally likely.

mcqs.q: Two pea plants heterozygous for two unlinked genes (RrYy) are crossed. Why is the expected phenotypic ratio among their offspring 9:3:3:1?
options: The 16 cells of the Punnett grid contain four genotypes in the proportions 9:3:3:1, and each of these genotypes gives a different phenotype
Each parent makes four types of gamete and these combine with the single gamete type of the other parent in equal numbers, giving 9:3:3:1
Each gene independently gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive, and multiplying the probabilities gives 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 for the four phenotype combinations
Alleles inherited together stay together, so each parent makes only RY and ry gametes and these combine to give the four phenotype classes
mcqs.explain: Because the genes assort independently, the chance of round is 3/4 and of yellow 3/4, so round yellow is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; round green and wrinkled yellow are each 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; wrinkled green is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. The same result comes from a 16-cell Punnett grid of the four gamete types from each parent.
rationales: A student who reads 9:3:3:1 as a genotypic ratio picks this. The grid contains nine different genotypes; 9:3:3:1 appears only when they are grouped by phenotype, the 9 class alone containing four genotypes.

A student who has confused the two dihybrid crosses picks this. Four gamete types meeting a single gamete type describes the test cross with a double homozygous recessive, which gives 1:1:1:1; here both parents make four gamete types.

Because the genes assort independently, the chance of round is 3/4 and of yellow 3/4, so round yellow is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; round green and wrinkled yellow are each 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; wrinkled green is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. The same result comes from a 16-cell Punnett grid of the four gamete types from each parent.

A student who thinks maternal and paternal alleles travel as sets picks this. Two gamete types from each parent would give only two phenotypes (round yellow and wrinkled green) in a 3:1 pattern, from three genotypes; independent assortment produces four gamete types, which is what generates the four phenotype classes in the 9:3:3:1 ratio.

mcqs.q: Mendel's second law predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio in the F2 of a dihybrid cross, yet a cross involving two genes close together on the same chromosome gives a ratio far from this. What does this show about the law?
options: The law is universal, so the unexpected ratio must be the result of new mutations or of errors made in scoring the offspring
The law still applies because all genes assort independently; the unexpected ratio must arise from unequal survival of the different offspring
The law applies only to autosomal genes, so this deviation shows that the two genes must be located on one of the two sex chromosomes
The law applies only when genes are on different chromosomes or far enough apart to recombine freely; all biological laws have exceptions
mcqs.explain: Mendel's second law applies only if genes are on different chromosomes or are far enough apart on one chromosome for recombination rates to reach 50%. Linked genes are a genuine exception, and students should recognize that there are exceptions to all biological laws under certain conditions.
rationales: A student who has learned the law without its conditions picks this. The deviation is real and repeatable: genes close together on one chromosome are inherited together, and no scoring error or mutation is needed to explain it.

A student who believes every gene assorts independently picks this. Genes on the same chromosome do not assort independently, because their alleles travel together unless crossing over separates them, so the ratio changes with no difference in survival.

A student who equates linkage with sex linkage picks this. Two genes close together on any chromosome, including an autosome, are linked; the stem says nothing about sex chromosomes, and autosomal linkage is the common case.

Mendel's second law applies only if genes are on different chromosomes or are far enough apart on one chromosome for recombination rates to reach 50%. Linked genes are a genuine exception, and students should recognize that there are exceptions to all biological laws under certain conditions.

mcqs.q: In a genome database, a student finds that a human gene has its locus on chromosome 11 and that a second gene has its locus a few thousand base pairs away on the same chromosome; each record names a different polypeptide product. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The two genes are linked, because their loci are in close proximity on the same chromosome, and each codes for its own polypeptide
The two records must describe alleles of one gene, because different sequences at nearby positions are alternative forms of the same gene
The two genes are not linked, because gene linkage applies only to genes that are carried on the X chromosome
The positions given are true only for the person whose genome was sequenced, since the locus of a gene varies between people
mcqs.explain: A locus is the specific position of a gene on a chromosome, and a database record gives the chromosome, the position and the polypeptide product. Two genes whose loci are close together on the same chromosome are linked and their alleles tend to be inherited together.
rationales: A locus is the specific position of a gene on a chromosome, and a database record gives the chromosome, the position and the polypeptide product. Two genes whose loci are close together on the same chromosome are linked and their alleles tend to be inherited together.

A student who thinks alleles sit at different positions picks this. All alleles of a gene share one locus; two loci with two different polypeptide products are two different genes, however close together they lie.
A student who equates linkage with sex linkage picks this. Linkage means two loci are on the same chromosome; chromosome 11 is an autosome, so this is autosomal linkage.

A student who thinks gene position varies between individuals picks this. The locus of a human gene is the same in every person; people differ in which alleles they carry at that locus, not in where it is.

mcqs.q: In a fruit fly the loci for body colour and wing shape are on the same autosome. A fly inherited one chromosome carrying the alleles G and W and the homologous chromosome carrying g and w, shown as G W and g w beside two vertical lines. Why does this fly not produce GW, Gw, gW and gw gametes in equal numbers?
options: The two genes are permanently joined together on the chromosome, so only GW and gw gametes can ever be formed by this fly
The alleles on each chromosome are passed on together unless crossing over between the loci separates them, which occurs in only some meioses
Because the genes are linked they must be on the X chromosome, so only female flies are able to produce the recombinant gametes
Because the fly received G and W from one parent and g and w from the other, the alleles from each parent stay together as a set in its gametes
mcqs.explain: Linked alleles fail to assort independently because they are on the same DNA molecule. GW and gw gametes are the majority; Gw and gW recombinant gametes arise only when a chiasma forms between the two loci in prophase I, and the closer the loci the less often that happens.
rationales: A student who takes 'linked' to mean inseparable picks this. Crossing over between the loci exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids, so recombinant Gw and gW gametes are produced, though at less than 50%.

Linked alleles fail to assort independently because they are on the same DNA molecule. GW and gw gametes are the majority; Gw and gW recombinant gametes arise only when a chiasma forms between the two loci in prophase I, and the closer the loci the less often that happens.
A student who equates linkage with sex linkage picks this. The stem states the loci are on an autosome; autosomal linkage has nothing to do with the sex chromosomes or the sex of the fly.

A student who thinks alleles from the same parent travel as a set picks this. Alleles stay together here because the two loci are on the same chromosome, not because of their parental origin; for unlinked genes the parental combinations are broken up by independent assortment, and even for linked genes crossing over produces some recombinants.

mcqs.q: A fly heterozygous for two linked genes (AaBb), which inherited the alleles A and B on one chromosome and a and b on the other, is test-crossed with an aabb fly. The offspring are 42 AaBb, 38 aabb, 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb. Which offspring are the recombinants, and what produced them?
options: The 42 AaBb and 38 aabb, because these offspring differ in genotype from the homozygous recessive parent
None of them, because two genes that are linked cannot give rise to any new combinations of their alleles
The 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb, produced by crossing over between the two loci in the heterozygous parent
All four classes, since a test cross of a double heterozygote gives four recombinant types in a 1:1:1:1 ratio
mcqs.specStatementText: Spotting recombinants in a test cross
mcqs.explain: The aabb parent contributes only ab gametes, so each offspring genotype reveals the gamete from the heterozygote. AB and ab gametes give the parental classes (42 and 38); Ab and aB gametes, formed only when crossing over occurs between the loci, give the two smaller recombinant classes (11 and 9, a recombination frequency of 20%).
rationales: A student who reads 'recombinant' as 'different from a parent' picks this. Recombinants have new combinations of the heterozygote's alleles; AaBb received the parental AB chromosome and aabb the parental ab chromosome, so both are parental classes.

A student who thinks linkage is absolute picks this. Crossing over between the loci in some meioses produces Ab and aB gametes, and these recombinants are visible here as the 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb offspring.

The aabb parent contributes only ab gametes, so each offspring genotype reveals the gamete from the heterozygote. AB and ab gametes give the parental classes (42 and 38); Ab and aB gametes, formed only when crossing over occurs between the loci, give the two smaller recombinant classes (11 and 9, a recombination frequency of 20%).

A student who applies the unlinked test-cross ratio to every dihybrid picks this. The 1:1:1:1 ratio requires independent assortment; here the two classes of 42 and 38 far exceed the classes of 11 and 9, which is the pattern of linked genes with a minority of recombinants.

mcqs.q: A cross between two double heterozygotes gives 160 F2 offspring: 95 show both dominant traits, 28 show the first dominant and the second recessive, 30 show the first recessive and the second dominant, and 7 show both recessive traits. The critical value of chi-squared at p = 0.05 is 7.815 for 3 degrees of freedom and 9.488 for 4 degrees of freedom. What is the outcome of a chi-squared test against a 9:3:3:1 ratio?
options: Expected numbers are 90, 30, 30 and 10; chi-squared is about 1.3, below 7.815, so the difference is significant and the two genes are linked
Expected numbers are 9, 3, 3 and 1; chi-squared is far above 9.488 for 4 degrees of freedom, so the null hypothesis must be rejected
Expected numbers are 90, 30, 30 and 10; chi-squared is about 1.3, below 7.815, so the null hypothesis that the genes are linked is accepted
Expected numbers are 90, 30, 30 and 10; chi-squared is about 1.3, below 7.815, so the null hypothesis is not rejected and the data fit 9:3:3:1
mcqs.specStatementText: Chi-squared: do the numbers fit the ratio?
mcqs.explain: Expected = 160 × 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16 = 90, 30, 30, 10. Chi-squared = 25/90 + 4/30 + 0/30 + 9/10 = 0.28 + 0.13 + 0 + 0.90 = 1.31. With four classes there are 3 degrees of freedom; 1.31 is below 7.815, so the difference is not significant at p = 0.05 and the observed results are consistent with independent assortment.
rationales: A student who thinks a value below the critical value indicates a significant difference picks this. Significance requires chi-squared to exceed the critical value; 1.3 is far below 7.815, so the data do not differ significantly from 9:3:3:1.

A student who uses the ratio itself as the expected numbers and sets degrees of freedom equal to the number of classes picks this. Expected numbers must be scaled to the sample total of 160, and four classes give 3 degrees of freedom, not 4.

A student who takes the null hypothesis to be the interesting claim picks this. The null hypothesis states there is no significant difference from the expected ratio, meaning the genes assort independently; a small chi-squared retains that hypothesis and gives no support for linkage.

Expected = 160 × 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16 = 90, 30, 30, 10. Chi-squared = 25/90 + 4/30 + 0/30 + 9/10 = 0.28 + 0.13 + 0 + 0.90 = 1.31. With four classes there are 3 degrees of freedom; 1.31 is below 7.815, so the difference is not significant at p = 0.05 and the observed results are consistent with independent assortment.

mcqs.q: A student carries out a chi-squared test on the F2 offspring of a dihybrid cross. Which statement about the test is correct?
options: The null hypothesis is that observed and expected numbers do not differ significantly, and the F2 counted is a sample of the population
The null hypothesis is that the two genes are linked, so that the observed numbers will differ from those expected from the predicted ratio
If the calculated chi-squared value is below the critical value at p = 0.05, the null hypothesis has been proved to be true
The number of degrees of freedom equals the number of phenotype classes, so a cross that produces four classes has four degrees of freedom
mcqs.specStatementText: Chi-squared: do the numbers fit the ratio?
mcqs.explain: The null hypothesis states there is no difference beyond chance between observed and expected results. Statistical testing uses a sample to represent a population: here the sample is the F2 generation that was counted, just as in many experiments the sample is a set of replicated measurements.
rationales: The null hypothesis states there is no difference beyond chance between observed and expected results. Statistical testing uses a sample to represent a population: here the sample is the F2 generation that was counted, just as in many experiments the sample is a set of replicated measurements.

A student who expects the hypothesis under test to be the interesting claim picks this. The null hypothesis is the hypothesis of no difference; linkage, which would produce a difference, belongs to the alternative hypothesis.

A student who upgrades 'not rejected' to 'proved' picks this. A small chi-squared shows the data are consistent with the expected ratio; it does not prove the null hypothesis, and a larger sample could still reveal a difference.

A student who sets degrees of freedom to the most obvious number picks this. Degrees of freedom are the number of classes minus one, because once the total is fixed only three of the four class sizes are free to vary, so the critical value is read for 3.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic D3.2 Inheritance

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Crosses involving linked genes are limited to the test cross (double heterozygote × double homozygous recessive), in which each offspring phenotype reveals the gamete received from the heterozygous parent. No item asks for the outcome of a cross between two double heterozygotes for linked genes, and no item converts a recombination frequency into map units or asks for the order of genes on a chromosome.

The database exploration itself cannot be carried out in a text-only item, so the skill is tested through its outcome: the meaning of a locus, what a database record of a human gene gives (chromosome, position and polypeptide product) and the consequence of two loci being on different chromosomes or close together on the same chromosome. No item asks for the name of a particular database or for the exact chromosomal coordinates of any human gene.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
